# Independent audit of joint cap stress and normal rotations

Audited notes:

* `candidate 5e600a897e2488c6`
* `candidate cda9653e9d3e6d40`
* the restricted facet-preserving perturbation class in
  `candidate 21db6cba533d25dc`, Section 3

The new conditional identities pass independent audit. Their hypotheses
remain an attained fixed-nonhollow-projection minimum in a finite-facet
class, with all fibers of positive \(d\)-volume. This audit does not prove
the missing per-group bound, remove the zero-fiber alternative, or address
an arbitrary hollow projection.

## 1. Compression and the assigned covering constraints

Each minimal positive continuous-normal circuit has positive weights
\(\rho_j\), \(\sum_j\rho_ju_j=0\), and rank \(k-1\). If its nullspace
had dimension greater than one, a small perturbation of a positive
dependence would make one coefficient zero while keeping the others
nonnegative, contradicting minimality. Thus the rank assertion is valid.

The cap contact equations at the anchor give \(h_i=A_i\cdot z_i\).
The projected condition \(A_i\cdot z\ge h_i\) makes the weighted sum of
cap margins nonnegative independently of the continuous coordinate.
Therefore that entire fiber plane is covered by the circuit. The case
\(A_i=0\) gives \(h_i=0\) and covers every fiber plane.

Finite projected compression is valid. The open complement of each
projected covering halfspace can be replaced by a closed halfspace with
the same trace on the finite set \(P\). Insert \(\operatorname{conv}P\)
and apply Doignon; lattice convexity guarantees that its integer points
are exactly \(P\). At most \(2^n\) original groups still cover \(P\).
Degenerate whole-space groups can be handled directly.

A nondeep group cannot cover an entire deepest fiber, since each of its
caps has mass strictly below \(\beta M\). Such a cover would contain a
deepest point in one of these small caps. Consequently only selected
deep-origin groups are needed for the deepest indices. Adding each
nondeep fiber's own slack group and making one fixed assignment for every
index gives the advertised complete cover.

For every feasible change of the cap coefficients, the linear constraints
\[
 C_{ip}=\sum_j\rho_{ij}(v_{ij}\cdot p-b_{ij})\ge0
\]
retain that cover of \(P\times\mathbb R^d\). They are not a surrogate for
an unverified covering property. This proves the joint maximum-volume
consequence in the same facet class.

The perturbation cone must be the restricted cone preserving each
fiber's original facet-normal set, as now stated explicitly in the note.
Its construction in the bounded-facet alternative is valid: the small
erosion normal fan has exactly those rays, and requiring linearity on
each individual fan prevents extra facet normals after using common
refinement coordinates. Common erosion, affine translations, and dilation
belong to this restricted class.

## 2. Exact joint derivative at a coincident facet

At the original parameters let the continuous cap normal be unit, write
its threshold in fiber \(z\) as \(t=b-v\cdot z\), and let
\[
 a=\delta h_z(n_F),\qquad
 \tau=\delta b-\delta v\cdot z
\]
when \(u\) is fixed. If the polytope lies inside the cap, its coincident
facet has outward normal \(-u\). The body's lower boundary in the
\(u\)-coordinate moves with speed \(-a\), while the cap boundary moves
with speed \(\tau\). The retained volume contribution is therefore
\[
 |F|\min(a,-\tau).
\]
Its two linear pieces convexify to
\(\theta|F|a-(1-\theta)|F|\tau\). If the polytope lies outside the cap,
the facet has outward normal \(u\), and the contribution is
\[
 |F|\max(a-\tau,0),
\]
whose convexified pieces give
\(\theta|F|a-\theta|F|\tau\).

These calculations prove that the effective section coefficient is
\((1-\theta)|F|\) in the inside case and \(\theta|F|\) in the outside
case, with precisely the **same** \(\theta\) as in the shape derivative.
Thus the parameter terms are
\[
 \delta v\cdot\sum_zs_z z-\delta b\sum_zs_z.
\]
They do not use independently chosen boundary fractions. The old
strict-erosion argument remains valid since \(\delta v=\delta b=0\)
there, and every positive active cap has a fixed facet portion strictly
inside it.

## 3. Farkas signs, transport, contact, and exact normalization

The objective covector equals the cap covectors minus nonnegative
multiples of the active support and coverage rows. Its coefficients in
the free variables \(b_{ij}\) and \(v_{ij}\) are zero. Since
\(\partial C_{ip}/\partial b_{ij}=-\rho_{ij}\) and
\(\partial C_{ip}/\partial v_{ij}=\rho_{ij}p\), these equations are
exactly
\[
 \lambda_{ij}S_{ij}=\rho_{ij}t_i,
 \qquad
 \lambda_{ij}\sum_zs_{ijz}z
          =\rho_{ij}\sum_p\eta_{ip}p,
 \qquad t_i=\sum_p\eta_{ip}.
\]
The sign of the coverage multipliers is therefore correct.

Each deep-origin cap has a positive section through the interior of its
own anchor fiber, so \(S_{ij}>0\) for every admissible trace. A stressed
group has all \(\lambda_{ij}>0\); a group with \(t_i=0\) has none.
Slack groups have \(\lambda=0\), forcing \(t_i=0\) and all their
nonnegative \(\eta\) to vanish. Only the at most \(2^n\) compressed
deep-origin groups can therefore carry stress.

For a stressed group, division gives the common integer section
barycenter
\[
 \bar z_i=\frac{\sum_zs_{ijz}z}{S_{ij}}
          =\frac{\sum_p\eta_{ip}p}{t_i}.
\]
Complementarity gives \(A_i\cdot\bar z_i=h_i\).

The critical-cap contact argument is valid. A globally deepest point
cannot lie strictly inside any cap of mass \(\beta M\): shifting that
cap inward through the point removes a positive strip from its own
positive-volume fiber, contradicting its depth. Thus all its critical
cap margins are nonpositive. At every assigned deepest index, their
positive weighted sum is nonnegative by coverage. Hence their sum and
each margin are zero. This common contact holds even before restricting
to indices with \(\eta_{ip}>0\).

The signed offsets consequently cancel group by group:
\[
 \sum_{j,z}\lambda_{ij}(b_{ij}-v_{ij}\cdot z)s_{ijz}
    =t_i\sum_j\rho_{ij}(b_{ij}-v_{ij}\cdot\bar z_i)=0.
\]
Substitution into the already audited shape Euler identity yields
\(\sum_{i,j}\lambda_{ij}=1/\beta\).

Joint homothety independently checks this normalization: scale all
continuous bodies and all \((v,b)\) by \(q\), leaving \(u\) fixed.
Every cap mass and total volume scale by \(q^d\). All active homogeneous
support and coverage rows vanish on this direction. At a coincident
facet the two derivative pieces agree along the homothety, so every
convexified trace gives the same value. Evaluating the stress is valid
even though an expanding homothety need not satisfy the fixed budgets;
a linear covector identity can be evaluated on any direction in its
coordinate space.

## 4. Normal rotations and compact trace moment sets

Allow \(u_j\) to vary in the linear space
\(\sum_j\rho_ju_j=0\). The original nonzero columns and a nonzero
\((k-1)\)-minor persist under small perturbations. The fixed dependence
keeps the rank at most \(k-1\), so these variations preserve the minimal
positive circuit locally. Unit length need not be preserved; unit normals
are used only at the differentiation point.

The cap displacement at a point \(x\) of a coincident facet is now
\[
 \tau(x)=\delta b-\delta v\cdot z-\delta u\cdot x.
\]
The same two formulas become integrals of
\(\min(a,-\tau(x))\) or \(\max(a-\tau(x),0)\). Their branches can change
within a facet, so one must use a measurable \(\theta(x)\in[0,1]\), as
the new note does. The shape coefficient uses \(\int_F\theta\), while
the cap coefficients use the mass and first moment of the corresponding
effective measure \((1-\theta)\mathcal H_{d-1}|_F\) or
\(\theta\mathcal H_{d-1}|_F\). These are coupled by one trace.

The admissible mass/first-moment sets are compact and convex. Weak limits
of measures dominated by the fixed finite facet measure remain dominated;
their densities consequently remain between zero and one. Continuity of
mass and first moments on the compact facet gives the asserted compact
finite-dimensional sets. Together with the fixed transverse terms these
produce compact convex cap-gradient sets.

The actual one-sided derivative belongs to a choice of these pointwise
branches and is bounded above by the support function of this gradient
set. No assumption of ordinary differentiability at a coincident facet
has entered the argument.

## 5. Closed dual cone and normalized rotational stress

Let \(D\) be the polyhedral admissible tangent cone, including the linear
normal-circuit constraints. Let \(\mathcal G\) be the compact union of
the active cap-gradient sets. The common erosion direction \(e\in D\)
satisfies \(g(e)\le-\epsilon_0<0\) uniformly for \(g\in\mathcal G\).
This follows from the fixed positive-area facet patch strictly inside
each active cap; arbitrary trace choices cannot remove that loss.

Consider a convergent sequence in
\(\operatorname{cone}(\mathcal G)+D^\circ\), where
\(D^\circ\) denotes covectors nonpositive on \(D\). Pairing with \(e\)
bounds the total coefficient of all cap generators, because the polar
part also pairs nonpositively with \(e\). The cap parts therefore lie in
a compact set and have a convergent subsequence. The residual polar
parts converge in the closed polyhedral cone \(D^\circ\). Thus the sum
cone is closed.

If the objective gradient lay outside it, separating the closed cone
would give a direction in \(D\) with positive objective derivative and
nonpositive pairing with every cap gradient. Adding a small positive
multiple of \(e\) makes all active cap derivatives strictly negative
while keeping objective growth. The resulting sufficiently small
perturbation is feasible and contradicts maximality. This proves the
normalized multiplier certificate without an abnormality gap.

## 6. Common full section centroid and the exact rank distinction

Let \(S_{ij}\), \(Z_{ij}\), \(X_{ij}\) be effective section mass,
integer first moment, and continuous first moment. The new normal
equations have a group vector multiplier \(q_i\) and read
\[
 \lambda_{ij}X_{ij}=\rho_{ij}q_i.
\]
Combining with the threshold and integer-normal equations gives the
same full centroid for every cap in a stressed group:
\[
 \left(\frac{Z_{ij}}{S_{ij}},\frac{X_{ij}}{S_{ij}}\right)
     =\left(\frac{\sum_p\eta_{ip}p}{t_i},\frac{q_i}{t_i}\right).
\]
Every effective section measure is positive and supported on its actual
cap section in \(C\). Its centroid belongs to \(C\) and to that affine
cap plane. The common centroid therefore lies on all group cap planes.

The convex combination of deepest centers carrying \(\eta\) has the
same integer projection and also lies on all these planes. Subtracting
the plane equations gives exactly
\[
 \bar x_i-\frac{\sum_p\eta_{ip}x_p}{t_i}
       \in\bigcap_j\ker u_{ij}.
\]
For \(k_i=d+1\), the rank is \(d\) and this kernel is zero. The common
section centroid is then the transported deepest-point combination.
Convexity of halfspace-depth regions gives depth at least \(\beta\),
and its membership in a critical cap of mass \(\beta M\) gives depth
at most \(\beta\). Thus the claimed exact ambient depth is justified.

For a deficient circuit the common-kernel ambiguity is real in the
equations. The note correctly makes no identification with the chosen
deepest-point combination in that case.

Finally, variable positive circuit weights add no geometric freedom:
replace each cap coefficient triple by \(\rho'_j/\rho_j\) times that
triple. This positive scaling preserves the cap, converts the
\(\rho'\)-dependence to the fixed \(\rho\)-dependence, and preserves the
projected covering expressions. Nonunit normal parameters make this a
legitimate local reparameterization. It does not require an additional
constraint qualification for bilinear weight/normal equations.

The multiplier normalization, common centroids, and contact relations are
therefore established under the stated hypotheses. A bound on a stressed
group's multiplier sum remains a distinct unproved step.
